items.title: Le torri dell’Eur a Roma sono state recuperate dopo quasi vent’anni di abbandono
items.summary: Dal 2027 ospiteranno la sede centrale dell’Agenzia delle Entrate, il restauro è costato 250 milioni di euro
items.content:
Lunedì a Roma sono state inaugurate le tre torri dell’Eur, rimesse a nuovo dopo un abbandono di quasi vent’anni, e dopo che per decenni avevano ospitato il ministero delle Finanze. Le ha restaurate Cassa Depositi e Prestiti, la società controllata dal ministero dell’Economia che ne è proprietaria, con un investimento da 250 milioni di euro. Dal 2027 le tre torri ospiteranno la sede centrale dell’Agenzia delle Entrate.

Il complesso è formato da cinque edifici: tre torri di 17 piani, alte circa 65 metri, due corpi più bassi e una struttura che li collega. In tutto sono circa 60mila metri quadrati di uffici, a cui si aggiungono oltre 21.700 metri quadrati di spazi sotterranei. Le tre torri ora sono rivestite di vetro e pietra, mentre i corpi bassi sono rivestiti di travertino, la pietra chiara usata in molti edifici dell’Eur e anche in molti edifici storici di Roma (è il materiale con cui venne costruito il Colosseo).

Le torri si trovano all’Eur, il quartiere di Roma Sud progettato negli anni Trenta per ospitare l’esposizione universale del 1942, che poi non si tenne a causa della guerra (EUR era un acronimo che stava per Esposizione Universale Roma). Dopo la guerra il quartiere fu completato e diventò soprattutto un quartiere di uffici, dove furono costruite le nuove sedi di diverse istituzioni. L’idea iniziale era di spostare progressivamente tutte o quasi le sedi dei ministeri, per decongestionare il centro storico, ma un vero decentramento amminsitrativo non si realizzò mai davvero.

Il progetto della sede del ministero delle Finanze fu affidato all’architetto romano Cesare Ligini, uno dei principali esponenti del razionalismo, la corrente architettonica che privilegiava forme geometriche semplici e funzionali. Per questo le torri sono conosciute anche come “torri Ligini”.

Il ministero rimase nelle torri per circa trent’anni, fino alla fine degli anni Novanta. Nei primi anni Duemila, quando ormai gli edifici erano vuoti, lo Stato decise di venderli e furono comprati per circa 500 milioni di euro da una società partecipata per metà dal ministero dell’Economia e per l’altra metà da Alfiere, una società che riuniva diversi imprenditori e costruttori.

Per alcuni anni si pensò di demolire le torri e costruire al loro posto un complesso residenziale progettato da Renzo Piano. Nel 2007, durante il mandato da sindaco di Walter Veltroni, furono smontate le facciate: secondo diverse ricostruzioni, quell’intervento serviva a evitare un vincolo di tutela sui palazzi, che avrebbe impedito di demolirli e ricostruirli. Il progetto residenziale però fu abbandonato, sia per altri vincoli architettonici sia per la crisi del mercato immobiliare, e si decise che le torri sarebbero rimaste destinate a uffici.

Dopo anni di abbandono e vari tentativi di metterci sedi di grandi gruppi come TIM e Ferrovie dello Stato, il recupero si è sbloccato solo nel 2022, quando il progetto è passato a Cassa Depositi e Prestiti, che gestisce le torri attraverso la sua società di gestione immobiliare CDP Real Asset SGR. Il cantiere è durato circa quattro anni. L’Agenzia delle Entrate dovrebbe trasferirsi nelle torri nel corso del 2027.

Durante la cerimonia di inaugurazione, il sindaco di Roma Roberto Gualtieri ha definito le torri «un esempio importante della rigenerazione che vogliamo promuovere a Roma: recuperare il patrimonio esistente, coniugando qualità, sostenibilità e innovazione», e ha collegato il recupero delle torri ad altri progetti in corso nel quartiere: il laghetto dell’Eur, che secondo il sindaco a breve diventerà balneabile , e il museo della Civiltà Romana, che dovrebbe riaprire all’inizio del 2027.

items.title: L’Arabia Saudita messa alle strette dagli huthi
items.summary: Il regno è costretto a fare i conti con una guerra da cui pensava di essersi sfilato. E scopre che delegare la propria sicurezza a Washington è stato un errore Leggi
items.content:
In questi giorni il principe ereditario dell’Arabia Saudita Mohammed bin Salman , teoricamente uno degli uomini più potenti del mondo, vive in palazzi pieni di bunker, circondato da una scorta scelta con estrema cura. Il suo regno, che sogna modernità e grandezza, ha dovuto interrompere i collegamenti aerei con il resto del mondo, mentre le ambasciate straniere consigliano prudenza ai loro cittadini. Il 12 ottobre a Riyad si è aperta una conferenza petrolifera internazionale senza la partecipazione dei dirigenti delle più grandi aziende del settore.

“Nel dizionario saudita la parola ‘paura’ non esiste”, ha dichiarato un dirigente del regno wahhabita. Sarà anche così, ma di sicuro c’è un dilemma strategico, perché l’Arabia Saudita deve affrontare una minaccia che non riesce a contenere.

Parlo degli huthi del vicino Yemen , all’origine della situazione che ho appena descritto. I miliziani sostenuti dall’Iran dispongono di un arsenale missilistico che negli ultimi giorni hanno usato per colpire l’aeroporto di Riyad, con un bilancio di tredici morti e trecento feriti. In precedenza erano stati presi di mira altri obiettivi, tra cui un Airbus fortunatamente vuoto.

L’ostilità tra gli huthi e l’Arabia Saudita non nasce oggi. Uno dei primi atti di bin Salman dopo essere stato nominato principe ereditario, nel 2015, è stato scatenare una guerra contro il gruppo. È stato un conflitto tanto impietoso quanto inconcludente, terminato con la ritirata saudita dallo Yemen nel 2022. La ripresa delle ostilità va inquadrata nel contesto più ampio della guerra in Iran scatenata lo scorso febbraio dagli Stati Uniti e da Israele, che ha ormai coinvolto la penisola arabica.

Gli huthi sono legati a Teheran, e l’escalation delle ultime settimane rientra in una logica precisa. L’obiettivo dell’ offensiva su Bab el Mandeb (l’equivalente sul mar Rosso dello stretto di Hormuz, al confine tra il sultanato dell’Oman e l’Iran) è quello di impedire all’Arabia Saudita di esportare petrolio, sfuggendo al controllo iraniano sul golfo Persico.

Il regno saudita non sembra in grado di rispondere agli attacchi. Una delle cause di questa incapacità è che la protezione statunitense, concessa all’Arabia Saudita nel 1945 , non sembra più credibile. L’11 ottobre, dopo gli attacchi contro gli aeroporti, Donald Trump ha dichiarato che potrebbe intervenire in aiuto di Riyad contro gli huthi, ma considerando che mancano tre settimane alle elezioni di metà mandato è improbabile che il presidente statunitense abbia voglia di entrare in un’altra guerra.

I sauditi, dunque, non hanno altra scelta se non quella di rientrare in un conflitto da cui pensavano di essersi sfilati per dedicarsi ai progetti faraonici del principe, attualmente sospesi o minacciati. Per questo motivo il regno cerca alleanze, soprattutto tra i firmatari del cosiddetto patto della Mecca (Turchia e Pakistan, che però non hanno manifestato grande entusiasmo) e con gli Emirati Arabi Uniti, con cui i rapporti sono piuttosto freddi.

La grande lezione, per l’Arabia Saudita, è che delegare la propria sicurezza agli Stati Uniti, pensando di non essere coinvolta dal conflitto con l’Iran, è stato un grave errore. Ora Riyad ne paga il prezzo, e dovrà rivedere i propri piani strategici.

items.title: La prima ministra del Marocco Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri ha fatto una coalizione con quattro partiti per formare il nuovo governo
items.content:
Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, nuova prima ministra del Marocco, ha fatto un accordo con quattro partiti per formare il governo: oltre al Partito dell’Autenticità e della Modernità (PAM), di cui lei è una dirigente e che è di orientamento progressista e vicino alla monarchia, la coalizione comprenderà Istiqlal, partito nazionalista e conservatore, e i partiti di orientamento socialdemocratico Unione Socialista delle Forze Popolari (USFP) e Partito del Progresso e del Socialismo (PPS). Il PAM era arrivato primo alle elezioni parlamentari del 23 settembre e aveva ottenuto 97 seggi su 395.

I quattro partiti che formeranno il nuovo governo hanno concordato di cominciare subito a preparare un programma condiviso e a scegliere i futuri ministri.

items.title: Burnham piccona la Brexit, 'un dovere riavvicinarsi all'Ue'
items.summary: 'Status quo non basta', dice il premier dopo denuncia 'interferenze russe' sul referendum
items.content:
Riavvicinarsi all'Ue perché "la Brexit ha fatto più male che bene" al Regno Unito e perché restare ancorati a "uno status quo" che non funziona sarebbe una "diserzione dal dovere". Andy Burnham rompe gli indugi e, a soli tre mesi dall'ascesa a Downing Street come successore alla testa del Labour dell'impopolare quanto ondivago Keir Starmer, lancia da Westminster la sfida destinata sulla carta a rimettere in discussione - per ora parzialmente - l'esito del referendum che 10 anni fa suggellò il divorzio dell'isola dal continente.

È tempo di "affrontare la realtà", ha tagliato corto il nuovo primo ministro alla Camera dei Comuni, nel primo giorno dopo la ripresa dei lavori parlamentari seguita alla pausa della stagione dei congressi di partito. Per poi annunciare l'avvio di un percorso "pragmatico" di revisione delle relazioni rabberciate con i 27 ricevute in eredità, a partire dal prossimo vertice fissato a Bruxelles il 20 novembre. E aggiungere - conscio dei sondaggi che negli ultimi tempi certificano sentimenti di crescente delusione, o Bregret, fra i suoi connazionali - come "la stragrande maggioranza dell'opinione pubblica si aspetti che venga colta l'opportunità" di un'inversione di rotta. Un cammino il cui esito finale il 56enne ex sindaco di Manchester lascia di fatto aperto per l'avvenire, dopo aver evocato già al congresso laburista di Liverpool l'intenzione di mettere sul tavolo "tutte le opzioni possibili". Nell'immediato, il nuovo obiettivo è negoziare un riallineamento su regole che - dall'agricoltura, alla pesca, all'energia - elimini alcuni degli ostacoli commerciali post Brexit (con vantaggi per l'economia britannica stimati nell'equivalente di10 miliardi di sterline l'anno entro il 2040); nonché il ritorno a "una condivisione dei dati" sul contrasto dell'immigrazione illegale. A più lungo termine tuttavia - pur mantenendo ferme in questa legislatura "le linee rosse" sul no alla libertà di movimento delle persone, al mercato unico e all'unione doganale, o escludendo al momento "qualsiasi referendum" bis su una riadesione tout court - l'orizzonte resta affacciato su una rimessa in discussione più radicale del divorzio: senza nessuna preclusione futura in effetti, rispetto alle scelte da sottoporre al voto in un prossimo manifesto elettorale. Poiché "il popolo è il boss". Da Bruxelles, la presidente della Commissione, Ursula von der Leyen, tende la mano via X con evidente soddisfazione: "Ue e Regno Unito - incoraggia - assieme hanno molto da guadagnare" La partita, però, ha anche una valenza tattica interna, sull'isola, nella battaglia per il consenso laddove Burnham ha solo iniziato a risalire la china dopo l'avvento a Number 10. Contrapposto in primis a due partiti di destra a guida brexiteer: i conservatori di Kemi Badenoch e soprattutto i populisti trumpiani di Reform Uk di Nigel Farage. Forze alle quali il primo ministro rinfaccia disinteresse non solo verso gli umori attuali "del grosso dei britannici", ma persino sui benefici di un riavvicinamento europeo rispetto ai loro dossier di bandiera: dal rilancio di una "crescita economica" asfittica, al coordinamento della difesa e della sicurezza (tanto più in tempi di minacce di guerra più o meno ibrida attribuite a Paesi quali Russia o Iran e d'incognite sulla 'special relationship' con gli Usa di Donald Trump). Fino al contenimento dell'immigrazione "clandestina". A sostegno della sua narrazione, Burnham non manca intanto di riesumare l'ombra del "tentativo d'interferenza" imputato a Mosca sul referendum del 2016: indicato per la prima volta da un capo di governo britannico alla stregua di un qualcosa di "chiaro" (per quanto senza effetti riconosciuti sul risultato "legittimo" della consultazione, come il successore di Starmer ha precisato in aula). Mentre Badenoch e Farage replicano a muso duro, accusandolo d'incoerenza e di voler "cercare di distrarre il Paese" dall'incapacità del governo di affrontare "i problemi reali" a costo di riaccendere "le divisioni". Oltre che di mettersi nelle mani dei negoziatori di Bruxelles: "Negoziatori duri", avverte la leader Tory, da cui non sarà l'ex sindaco di Manchester a strappare "un accordo migliore".

items.title: L’aeroporto di Riyad resterà chiuso fino a sabato a causa degli attacchi degli Houthi
items.content:
L’aeroporto Re Khalid di Riyad, la capitale dell’Arabia Saudita, resterà chiuso fino a sabato 17 ottobre. Dopo gli attacchi degli ultimi giorni rivendicati dagli Houthi , il gruppo politico e militare che governa parte dello Yemen e contro cui l’Arabia Saudita sta di fatto combattendo una guerra, le compagnie aeree hanno infatti cancellato i voli da e per Riyad.

L’aeroporto Re Khalid è il secondo aeroporto più trafficato del paese dopo quello di Gedda. Era chiuso da sabato scorso, giorno in cui c’era stato un attentato che aveva ucciso 13 persone e causato oltre 300 feriti, il più grave nel paese da oltre un decennio e il singolo attacco con più morti in un paese arabo del golfo Persico da quando a febbraio era cominciata la guerra in Medio Oriente. Domenica c’era stato un altro attacco in cui era stata uccisa una persona.

Gli Houthi sono un gruppo sciita alleato dell’Iran. Governano parte dello Yemen dal 2014, quando con un’operazione militare conquistarono la capitale Sana’a cacciando il governo internazionalmente riconosciuto e appoggiato dall’Arabia Saudita. Cominciò una lunga guerra civile, in cui i sauditi sostennero il governo yemenita. Nel 2022 fu raggiunta una tregua che ridusse notevolmente i combattimenti, senza però mettere fine al conflitto. Gli Houthi continuarono a controllare parte del paese.

Nelle scorse settimane i combattimenti si sono intensificati nuovamente: dopo alcuni attacchi degli Houthi, l’Arabia Saudita ha avviato una nuova offensiva in territorio yemenita.

items.title: Il “cessate il fuoco energetico” tra Ucraina e Russia non è mai esistito
items.summary: Era stato annunciato domenica da Trump, ma Zelensky non ne sapeva niente e gli attacchi russi intanto sono continuati
items.content:
Il “cessate il fuoco energetico” tra Russia e Ucraina annunciato domenica dal presidente statunitense Donald Trump non è mai entrato in vigore, e per quanto ne sappiamo non è nemmeno mai esistito. Né la Russia né l’Ucraina lo hanno confermato e nelle ore successive all’annuncio l’esercito russo ha continuato a bombardare le infrastrutture energetiche ucraine.

Lunedì il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha accusato la Russia di aver colpito almeno sei impianti energetici, provocando interruzioni nelle forniture di elettricità, e ha minacciato di rispondere agli attacchi se i bombardamenti russi continueranno. Il governo ucraino ha ribadito di essere disponibile a interrompere gli attacchi contro le infrastrutture energetiche russe, a condizione che la Russia faccia altrettanto.

La proposta di Trump si inserisce in una nuova crisi nei rapporti tra Stati Uniti e Ucraina, cominciata venerdì quando il presidente statunitense ha fatto un accordo con Putin per aumentare le esportazioni di gasolio russo e per cercare di ridurre i prezzi del carburante negli Stati Uniti. Da allora Trump ha fatto pressioni sull’Ucraina perché interrompesse gli attacchi contro le raffinerie russe, senza ottenere però una disponibilità equivalente dalla Russia.

Non è la prima volta che Trump annuncia un “cessate il fuoco energetico” senza che questo sia stato effettivamente concordato. Era già successo lo scorso 14 settembre e anche in quel caso i bombardamenti erano continuati.

items.title: Death threats and isolation - the cost of fighting sexual violence in Iraq
items.summary: Women say they share stories of abuse to highlight the issue, despite social pressure and safety fears.
items.content:
This story contains details of sexual violence which some readers may find upsetting

"Get out of the car!" screams a woman, accusing a driver of exposing himself and making obscene comments as she walked by. She is filming the scene in a busy Baghdad street on her phone, and the camera captures him resisting her attempts to open the door as she confronts him .

The video can be seen, with others like it, on the Instagram page of Iraqi women's rights activist Sarah Jassim. She posts them on behalf of women who complain about sexual abuse and harassment by Iraqi men and boys.

"Your camera is your weapon," she tells the BBC. "It's a way to document evidence in case a woman decides to sue her harasser, or at least it is a means to shame him."

One of the videos she posted led to the arrest of the alleged perpetrator, a policeman accused of harassing schoolgirls, she says.

Jassim says posting the videos is risky both for herself and for the women concerned. We have spoken to numerous victims of sexual abuse in Iraq who say that society often blames the victim.

"I have received death threats, and I have also been threatened with acid attacks," Jassim says. "I have been accused of inciting public indecency, because I encourage women to speak in a society that expects us to be silent."

She now barely leaves home, for her own safety, and instead spends hours playing with her dog.

There is a need for stricter laws, she argues, including laws that explicitly criminalise "harassment" and "gender-based violence" - terms that are currently absent from the penal code.

"Recognising the problem is the best way to address it," she says. "We need protection, abusers have to be deterred."

Many Iraqi women have told the BBC they felt failed by the justice and police systems. Pursuing legal action against a harasser or a rapist is a long path in Iraq, with complicated procedures, and uncertain results, according to a number of activists and lawyers we have spoken to.

Violence against women and girls in Iraq is "widespread and under-reported," according to a report in May by a UN committee on discrimination against women, which called for stronger legislation.

Among dozens of recommendations, it urged the authorities to repeal "discriminatory" laws that exonerate rapists if they marry their victims, and allow reduced sentences for murder in cases where a perpetrator was carrying out a so-called "honour killing".

Amal - not her real name - has been battling in court for about five years. She accuses her ex-husband of repeatedly raping their daughter - who was under 18 at the time - at gunpoint.

She recalls her daughter's harrowing account of the incident, when she says the father walked into the girl's room and laid his weapon on her bed. She says he told her: "No-one will hear you if I kill you."

Sexual abuse has long been seen as a taboo subject in Iraq. I have been in touch with many survivors who say that they prefer to hush it up, because of a potential family backlash. Others told us they were afraid to go to the police, for fear of social stigma and possible harassment. But Amal was determined to seek justice and rushed to police to report the incident.

"She had lots of bruises around her wrists, as he held her hands tight. Whenever she tried to scream, he would cover her mouth with his hands," Amal says.

Amal showed me medical documents, including DNA evidence, which support her account.

A further demonstration of her ex-husband's cruelty came, Amal says, when she heard him tell a family member to "wash off our disgrace" if he was arrested. The expression is used in Iraq to refer to so-called honour killings - carried out in the belief that a woman has compromised a family's reputation.

Amal says she believes the father threatened to put an end to his daughter's life "so the medical report would not be released and the assault would not be proven".

She says her ex-husband is on the run and the court case remains open.

"I fought all alone," says Amal, bursting into tears as she says her ex-husband hired several lawyers but she could not afford legal representation, and her family turned a blind eye to the situation.

She no longer has any faith that a court ruling will come in her favour. "I just want him to stay out of my way forever," she says, with a sigh of despair.

Amal's daughter is more fortunate than some women who have experienced domestic sexual abuse in Iraq, as she has a safe place to live.

Many survivors have no independent income and nowhere to go. Iraq has very few shelters for abused women.

Those we know of were established by an organisation co-founded by Yanar Mohammed, an internationally recognised women's rights advocate. Last March she was murdered outside her house in Baghdad by armed men. The perpetrators are still unknown.

Experts working for the UN Human Rights Council wrote in April that Mohammed had been receiving death threats and online abuse for years, which were "believed to come from extremist religious militia".

Activists repeatedly told us that targeted attacks on their colleagues have been on the rise in recent years.

Hanaa Edwar, another prominent women's rights activist, says she saw Mohammed just two days before she was killed. She says she has also been threatened.

"There are no laws, no protection, and no justice for women in Iraq," she tells me.

"The problem in Iraq is not that women stay silent. It is that when they speak, very little in the system is built to listen, Mustafa Saadoon, head of the Iraqi Observatory for Human Rights, tells the BBC.

"A woman who reports sexual violence has to get past her family first, then a police station, then a court, and at every one of those doors someone is likely to tell her to settle it quietly."

Among the Iraqi women who say they feel failed by the system is Samira - not her real name.

She tells the BBC that walking in the street puts her on the edge, after repeated harassments.

Once, she says a man "was watching a porn movie on his phone and put it in my face" on public transport.

In another incident in Baghdad, she says a man once followed her in his car for over 10 minutes. "It was extremely upsetting... I saw a police car. I went over and told them what had happened. They said they didn't have the authority to do anything."

Although her mother is loving and supportive, Samira does not share any stories of sexual harassment with her. "If I tell my family, they will immediately ask me not to leave home in order to stay safe," she says.

She has lost faith in state institutions: "Many men, including police officers, find nothing wrong with sexual harassment. If you are not a harasser, you are not a man, this is how they see it," she adds.

Many women I spoke to in Iraq even accused police of sexual harassment. I put the accusation to Muqdad Miri, a spokesman for Iraq's interior ministry.

"Cases of harassment involving police personnel happen but they are very few. They get a very harsh punishment, up to 10 years in prison and are dismissed," says Miri.

I put it to him that some women were now documenting harassment on social media because they were afraid to report it to police. He said they were posting on social media because it was easier than filing an official report, and because doing so has become a common way to draw attention to a cause.

I also put to him Samira's experience, in which she says an officer told her that he had no authority to stop harassment. Miri said Samira could have filed a complaint against this officer.

There are no reliable statistics for sexual violence or harassment in Iraq. Miri told me that police have received about 300 reports of sexual violence since the beginning of the year. However, he accepts that the real number of cases is higher: "Many cases never reach the police because of society, customs and traditions."

The stories of the women the BBC spoke to draw a picture of their battle not just against sexual violence itself, but against deeply entrenched mentalities and social beliefs that allow it to persist.

Edwar has been advocating for women's causes for over 50 years and her assessment is gloomy: "Twenty-three years after Saddam Hussein's regime was brought down, it seems we are going backwards regarding women's rights."

But both she and Jassim say they refuse to give up: "If all of us are going to get scared, no-one will change anything," says Sarah.

If you have been affected by issues involving sexual abuse and violence, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

items.title: Where the US midterm elections will be won and lost
items.summary: An in-depth look at the key polling, races and issues ahead of an election that will define Trump’s final two years as president.
items.content:
Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.

Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.

Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.

Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.

One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.

He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.

It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.

Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.

But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.

The current Republican majority in the House of Representatives, the lower chamber, is as thin as it gets - they have 218 representatives, which is the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them.

Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.

But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.

The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.

Of those 21 toss-ups, 15 are currently held by Republicans and six by Democrats. If the Democrats win five of those on top of 28 districts classed as likely or leaning Democratic, they will win the House.

Historically, the midterms see a high number of seats changing hands in the House, usually in a protest against the White House. The average number lost by the president's party is 27, according to data , external going back to 1934. Of those 23 elections, the president's party has only made gains in three.

The Republicans have a slightly stronger hold on the Senate. They hold 53 of the 100 seats while the Democrats have 45 and two independents who also vote with them.

Members of the Senate serve six-year terms so roughly a third are up for election every two years.

Thirty-five seats are up for grabs in November but analysis by the Cook Political Report suggests that only seven of them are toss-ups that could go either way.

Of those toss-ups, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus the four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.

They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.

And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.

But polls suggest they have a chance, even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.

Anthony Zurcher: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope

Trump pledged to "end inflation and make America affordable again" in his 2024 election campaign but the cost of living crisis is proving to be the key issue for voters.

The president proudly declared that gas was "now below $2.30 [£1.74] a gallon in most states" in his State of the Union address on 24 February. But the war with Iran began four days later, disrupting Middle Eastern energy supplies and causing gas to hit $4 (£3.03) in the US.

The war became increasingly unpopular as its consequences reverberated around the world and ultimately hit American consumers in the pocket. One poll carried out in August found 63% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of the situation.

Other issues that voters say are important to them include healthcare and immigration.

Trump has recently touted his policies around immigration as a big success, citing significantly lower border-crossing figures than in recent years.

Many Democratic candidates are focusing on the high costs of US health insurance and the impact of Trump's legislation on access to the healthcare system.

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?

Most signs point towards a successful midterms for the Democrats, but it wouldn't be the first time that Trump and his party have outperformed polls if they do win more seats than expected.

One of the few things in their favour is their huge financial advantage.

At the end of August, the Republican National Committee and its allied groups had more than $600m (£455m) cash on hand, while the Democrats had just under $400m (£303m).

On top of that, the Republicans also had more than $400m held by Trump's MAGA Inc group, the main fundraising and spending arm of the "Make America Great Again" political movement.

The Republicans are using that financial advantage to buy advertising.

More than $1bn worth of political ads were broadcast to US voters in September, according to research firm AdImpact , external . Republicans spent $200m more than the Democrats and outspent them in nearly all of the Senate races classed as toss-ups.

Trump will be hoping this late messaging blitz can help convince Republicans to get out and vote in November, boosting turnout and limiting the damage done to him and his party.

Whatever the result, attention will quickly turn to the next presidential election in 2028. Trump's unpopularity has dominated the midterms, but with him constitutionally unable to run for a third term the focus will shift to what the Democrats stand for, not just what they stand against.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

items.title: Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC
items.summary: In his first interview since being forced from his post, Gen Syrskyi speaks about Ukraine's future in the war.
items.content:
Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by killing so many of its men, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief has said in an interview with the BBC.

Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi made the comments in an exclusive interview, his first since he was dramatically forced from his post in the summer.

He addressed his sacking, disagreeing with his critics who declared him too "old school" to command Ukraine's new, technologically advanced forces.

He also pushed back against allegations made by soldiers who previously served under him, who told the BBC they were ordered to remain at their positions even when they were almost surrounded by Russians, leading to high losses.

Syrskyi said that Moscow's overall losses in the war were six times higher than Ukraine's. "If you count only dead, then it's up to 11 times," he added.

Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially release the numbers of their dead. Ukraine's military says it inflicted record losses this year on Russian soldiers in September, although that cannot be verified.

UK intelligence chiefs estimate Russia has lost around half a million men killed in Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. The US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies meanwhile believes , external Ukraine has lost up to 150,000 troops killed by June 2026.

He says this difference in death toll – as well as technological advances, and a strategy of attacking weak points in Russia's lines while containing their advances in other parts – accounts for the current stalemate at the front.

In the first six months of 2026, Russia managed overall to seize 61 sq km, the general said. "It's an indication that the front line has been stabilised."

The Institute for Study of War (ISW) has also confirmed this trend. One of its recent reports , external says that in September 2026, Moscow lost more territory than it took.

Syrskyi was appointed Ukraine's commander-in-chief in 2024. He had previously won praise for defending Kyiv at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and for leading the successful counteroffensive east of Kharkiv in the autumn of that year.

But President Volodymyr Zelensky fired Syrskyi this summer, amid a major disagreement with then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

Fedorov had said that instead of adapting to the realities of the changing war, the army under Syrskyi had blocked his initiatives.

Zelensky initially fired Fedorov, as tensions burst into the open between the two men. But mass street protests then forced the president to also fire Syrskyi, replacing him with Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43.

Syrskyi told the BBC that he had "disagreements" with Fedorov because the latter "didn't take into consideration the interests of the army" when procuring weapons and supplies.

Fedorov had created an "imbalance" in supplies, Syrskyi said. He had prioritised drones while overlooking key front-line kit such as unmanned ground vehicles, pick-up trucks and motorbikes. Even with drones, Syrskyi said, there were shortages as the army got only half of what they needed.

Fedorov was a popular young minister who was known for his digital and technological initiatives. Many contrasted him with Syrskyi, who critics thought was not fit to lead the new technological arms race with Russia.

But Syrskyi disagrees with such criticism. It was during his time the use of drones reached this new, unprecedented level, including deep strikes more than 2,000km (1,200 miles) behind enemy lines, he said. Ukraine was the first country to create the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch of armed forces, under his command: now, he said, drones account for 80% of Russia's losses.

Under his military leadership, however, Ukrainian troops undertook chaotic withdrawals from the eastern cities of Avdiivka and Vuhledar, and from around Pokrovsk.

Soldiers who spoke to the BBC in the past complained that they were ordered to remain at their positions at any costs. By the time they were told to pull back, it was often too late as they were almost surrounded by Russian troops.

Syrskyi does not deny that such situations occur on the front line. But he told the BBC that Ukraine was fighting against a far more powerful army.

In 2025, the ratio of jets and bombs was 18 to one in Moscow's favour, he said. In the same year, Russia had two-and-a-half times more artillery pieces and shells than Ukraine. And with four million militarily trained men who they can mobilise, Russian forces can create chances to push through, he argued.

One of Syrskyi's most famous operations was an incursion into Russia's Kursk region that started in August 2024. It ended with a dramatic retreat the following spring, which some soldiers described as "catastrophic". Syrskyi, however, insisted that the Kursk operation was "a necessity".

"In the summer 2024, Russian forces were pushing along all main directions on the front line with up to six times more troops than we had," he explained.

The Kursk incursion disrupted Russia's offensive and forced Moscow to redirect troops, giving Ukraine a respite and a chance for its stretched brigades in the east and south to recover, Syrskyi said.

He also had strong words for European allies who doubt that Russia may have territorial ambitions beyond Ukraine. He advised European partners to start preparing for the war now and "drop all illusions that [it] will not come".

He also said he believed Ukraine's war was going to become even more technological. There will be more robots, automated systems and artificial intelligence (AI). "Even ordinary weapons now get an AI-based control system to enhance their capabilities," he said.

Such technologies can give a new life to conventional weapons like tanks. Both Russia and Ukraine were now racing to develop "active systems of defence" to protect armoured vehicles, Syrskyi said.

But he insisted that "the human role will remain definitive [on the battlefield] because [people] will need to control those systems".

items.title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
items.summary: It comes after the armed group hit Riyadh's international airport and another facility, killing 13 people, in a significant escalation.
items.content:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.

"The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.

On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.

The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.

A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.

Explosions were heard again in Riyadh on Monday night, with the Saudi-led military coalition saying a ballistic missile had been intercepted and destroyed.

A Houthi spokesperson said the group had again targeted the airport.

Meanwhile, Qatar Airways has said it will temporarily suspend flights to Riyadh and the north-eastern city of Dammam.

Etihad Airways said it had cancelled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to "regional disruption".

King Khalid airport is expected to remain closed until Saturday.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said early on Tuesday that the Houthis had shot down what he described as a Saudi "reconnaissance drone".

Meanwhile, the official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed "two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Khamis Mushait", in a statement shared on Tuesday.

The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.

Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.

Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.

On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).

King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.

Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.

Meanwhile, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.

In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks.

"You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.

But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".

Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges.

"We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."

On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.

Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".

Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.

UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.

President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.

Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.

Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.

They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.

Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

One killed, 11 injured in second Houthi strike on Riyadh airport in two days

Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict

items.title: BBC's Orla Guerin travels with Yemen's southern national security forces through desert battlefield
items.summary: Orla Guerin travelled through Yemen, with forces loyal to its internationally recognised government, to a remote desert battlefield where Houthi rebels were dislodged just days ago.
items.content:
On Yemen's desert battlefield a war with global consequences is being waged.

The BBC's Orla Guerin saw the impact firsthand when she travelled with southern national security forces to frontline positions where they've been battling Houthi fighters.

Yemen's civil war over expanses of desert land has had devastating consequences for civilians and fighters.

One military hospital in Aden reported more than 50 casualties arriving in a single day – many with gunshot wounds, and several needing amputations.

items.title: Il Fondo monetario: “L’economia mondiale cresce ancora, ma aumentano i rischi”
items.summary: Le previsioni per il 2026 ritoccate dal 3 al 3,1%. L’Italia passa da una stima di +0,5% a +0,8%, ma resta debole in Europa. Frena la Francia
items.content:
BANGKOK – L’economia mondiale resiste alle guerre, alla crisi energetica e alle tensioni commerciali meglio di quanto si prevedesse soltanto tre mesi fa: quest’anno crescerà del 3,1%, con un lievissimo miglioramento rispetto al 3% previsto a luglio. Ma «questa capacità di resistenza è sotto pressione, con i rischi orientati al ribasso», avverte Silvana Tenreyro, nuova capo economista del Fondo monetario internazionale. E l’Italia, anche se vede arrivare una revisione al rialzo delle sue stime, resta tra i Paesi europei più lenti: il Pil aumenterà dello 0,8% quest’anno, rispetto allo 0,5% previsto a luglio, ma solo dello 0,6% nel 2027. È questa la fotografia del nuovo “World Economic Outlook”, presentato oggi a Bangkok.

L’economia globale pare per ora tenere e «sono due le forze fondamentali che determinano queste prospettive», spiega Tenreyro. «La prima è l’aumento dei prezzi dell’energia e delle altre materie prime provocato dalla guerra, che agisce come uno shock negativo dell’offerta globale. La seconda è il boom tecnologico, trainato soprattutto dall’intelligenza artificiale, che agisce come uno shock positivo della domanda». Ma la notizia non ottima è che «mentre queste due forze spingono l’attività economica in direzioni opposte, entrambe esercitano pressioni al rialzo sull’inflazione».

Il confronto tra le tre grandi aree economiche parla da solo. Gli Stati Uniti cresceranno del 2,3% sia quest’anno sia nel 2027, la Cina rallenterà dal 4,5 al 4%, mentre la zona euro si fermerà all’1,1% nel 2026 e all’1,2% nel 2027. Rispetto a luglio, le prospettive americane ed europee migliorano leggermente, mentre quelle cinesi si riducono. Ma il quadro non cambia: l’America continua a crescere a un ritmo doppio rispetto all’Europa, mentre la Cina corre, ma perde velocità.

A spiegare la resistenza americana sono soprattutto la solidità dei consumi, la spesa pubblica, condizioni finanziarie ancora favorevoli e gli investimenti tecnologici. Gli Stati Uniti subiscono inoltre un impatto diretto relativamente limitato della guerra in Medio Oriente, grazie alla loro posizione di esportatori netti di energia. Diverso il caso della Cina, dove il rallentamento riflette consumi interni deboli, investimenti in difficoltà e una crisi immobiliare ancora irrisolta. Le esportazioni continuano a sostenere l’attività, ma non bastano a compensare la debolezza della domanda interna. Pechino resta comunque, insieme all’India, uno dei principali motori della crescita asiatica.

Nell’eurozona, invece, le contraddizioni dell’economia mondiale si presentano senza filtri. La rachitica crescita europea, spiega il rapporto, dipende «dal persistente freno esercitato dai prezzi più elevati dell’energia e dalla debole fiducia dei consumatori». L’Europa importa energia, partecipa solo in misura limitata al grande ciclo degli investimenti nell’intelligenza artificiale e deve contemporaneamente affrontare il problema di bilanci pubblici sotto pressione. Un quadro non entusiasmante, a partire dall’Italia. Il miglioramento delle stime per quest’anno non cambia il problema di fondo: il Paese continua a crescere meno della media europea e nel 2027 è prevista una nuova frenata. Anche l’inflazione torna a mordere: dall’1,6% del 2025 al 3,3% di quest’anno, prima di scendere al 2,8% nel 2027. La disoccupazione dovrebbe invece ridursi dal 6,1% del 2025 al 5,6% quest’anno, per risalire leggermente al 5,8% nel prossimo.

A “tirare” è adesso soprattutto la Germania: dopo il quasi ristagno del 2025, con una crescita dello 0,2%, il Pil dovrebbe aumentare dell’1,3% quest’anno e dell’1,1% nel prossimo. Il miglioramento rispetto a luglio è significativo, soprattutto per il 2026, con sei decimali in più. Molto più difficile la situazione in Francia: Il Pil crescerà solo dello 0,4% quest’anno e dello 0,7% nel prossimo, due decimali meno delle previsioni di luglio in entrambi i casi. È il risultato peggiore tra le quattro principali economie dell’eurozona e arriva mentre Parigi deve affrontare il problema del risanamento dei conti pubblici. La Spagna resta invece l’eccezione europea. Madrid crescerà del 2,5% nel 2026 e dell’1,8% nel 2027. Il Fondo migliora di quattro decimali la previsione per quest’anno, confermando la forza di un’economia che non salva però la stabilità politica a Madrid.

Su tutte queste economie pesa poi l’inflazione, che nell’eurozona dovrebbe raggiungere il 3,1% nel 2026, prima di scendere al 2,8% nel 2027. E soprattutto il rialzo del costo del denaro. Tenreyro ne individua tre cause: la maggiore domanda prodotta dagli investimenti nell’intelligenza artificiale e dalla spesa pubblica, lo shock inflazionistico dell’energia e i premi più elevati che gli investitori chiedono per acquistare titoli di Stato. Toccherebbe alle banche centrali spingere sul freno, alzando i tassi: «In linea di principio la politica monetaria dovrebbe essere più restrittiva per assicurare che l’inflazione torni all’obiettivo». Ma di fronte a uno shock energetico, dice ancora Tenreyro, «si ottiene questo risultato limitando la domanda e quindi aggravando la caduta dell’attività economica provocata dallo shock stesso».

Sullo sfondo – per tutti - resta soprattutto il problema dei conti pubblici. «I Paesi con debiti e deficit elevati devono avviare un consolidamento fiscale e assicurarsi che i deficit e, in ultima analisi, il debito siano su una traiettoria discendente», afferma Tenreyro. Un’indicazione che riguarda direttamente anche l’Italia, sebbene non sia citata in modo esplicito: «L’aumento dei costi di finanziamento e dei pagamenti per interessi può sottrarre spazio alla spesa essenziale in altri settori e ridurre i margini di bilancio disponibili per affrontare shock futuri».

items.title: Watch: US man eyes pumpkin world record after fifth contest win
items.summary: Horticulture teacher Travis Gienger hauled his pumpkin from Minnesota to Half Moon Bay, California where he won the annual event.
items.content:
A five-time US giant pumpkin contest winner tells the BBC he'd "love" to break the world record for a second time.

Horticulture teacher Travis Gienger hauled his pumpkin from Minnesota to Half Moon Bay, California, for the annual pumpkin weighing event.

His whopping gourd took home the prize, tipping the scales at 2,389 pounds (1,083kg).

But Gienger says he's eyeing off a different prize – the world record title – which was set in England's south coast last week with a squash weighing in at 2,857 pounds (1,300kg).

As a previous holder of the world-record mantle, Gienger says he's focused on the challenge ahead.

items.title: La strategia di comunicazione dell’estrema destra israeliana
items.summary: Il video dei militanti della Global sumud flotilla maltrattati, pubblicato dal ministro Itamar Ben Gvir, è solo un esempio di come i partiti suprematisti cercano il consenso. La nuova puntata della serie video Dietro le immagini Leggi
items.content:
A maggio i militanti filopalestinesi della Global sumud flotilla sono stati umiliati dall’esercito israeliano di fronte alle telecamere. Il video dei maltrattamenti, pubblicato su X dal suprematista e razzista Itamar Ben Gvir , ministro della sicurezza nazionale, è solo un esempio della strategia di comunicazione aggressiva dell’estrema destra israeliana. Il caso ha suscitato un’ondata di indignazione internazionale, ma in patria è un metodo che trova consensi anche in vista delle elezioni del 27 ottobre.

Dietro le immagini è una serie della tv franco-tedesca Arte che ricostruisce la storia di una foto, di un video o di un’immagine, dalla sua creazione al suo impatto sul nostro modo di vedere il mondo. Proponendoci un’interpretazione che spinge ad andare oltre il primo sguardo.

items.title: Italy’s great wine heists: from winery cellars to the vaults of Michelin-starred restaurants
items.summary: The €5 million raid on Marchesi Antinori is only the latest in a long string of thefts
items.content:
Thirty thousand bottles have been stolen from the cellars of Marchesi Antinori in Cortona, Tuscany. At €5 million, it is the biggest wine theft in Italian history. The gang struck at night in a near-military operation, evading alarm systems, disabling security cameras and loading hundreds of cases onto lorries, making off with prized bottles from the 2023 vintage.

But it is only the latest chapter in a long series of attacks on the country’s most prestigious wine estates, from Montalcino to the Langhe, from the vaults of Michelin-starred restaurants to trucks loaded with pallets.

Organised crime is not after safes or share portfolios, but the “red gold” of Italian viticulture. These are top-quality products which, when stolen in bulk, can be stockpiled and resold on parallel markets across the Atlantic, in Eastern Europe and at clandestine auctions around the world, and even to Italian venues through underground sales channels.

In 2026, gangs repeatedly targeted Piedmont’s flagship producers, with two near-identical raids just months apart. In late June, the Banfi Piemonte winery in Strevi was ransacked, with more than 3,000 bottles of Alta Langa DOCG taken, among them the prestigious Cuvée Aurora and the Riserva 100 Mesi, along with entire pallets.

In September 2026, the same script played out at the historic Conterno Fantino estate in Monforte d’Alba, one of the Langhe’s most revered Barolo producers.

Working at night with their faces covered, the thieves used the winery’s own forklifts to load some 3,000 bottles of top-end Barolo (vintages 2021 and 2022, including magnums and jeroboams) in around three hours. The damage runs to hundreds of thousands of euros, and the job was carried out with cold logistical efficiency.

Across Italy, the robberies reveal a striking pattern of made-to-order raids. In the Langhe, they include Fontanafredda (about 170 cases, December 2015), Cordero di Montezemolo (250 cases, June 2016) and Parusso (120 cases, July 2016). In Montalcino, thieves hit Cupano (900 bottles, December 2016) and Col d’Orcia (1,000 bottles of Brunello, including vintages dating back to 1964, January 2017, with an estimated value of between €50,000 and €100,000).

Large-scale logistics have also been targeted: 16,000 bottles of fine wine were stolen from a warehouse in Modena (October 2015, about €100,000); 9,000 bottles of Masi’s Costasera Amarone were reported missing from a logistics warehouse in the Verona area in January 2023 (more than €315,000; in September 2004, 12,000 bottles of Amarone, worth around €250,000, had already been stolen from Masi’s own depot); and 16,000 bottles were taken from Enoitalia in Montebello Vicentino (€45,000, wines destined for Lidl supermarkets).

In February 2024, it was the turn of the Sergio Mottura winery in Civitella d’Agliano, in the province of Viterbo, where 6,000 bottles were carted off on pallets, with losses of more than €90,000. The most recent hits are those at Banfi in Strevi (more than 3,000 bottles of Alta Langa, valued at anywhere from tens of thousands to around €100,000, according to estimates) and Conterno Fantino in Monforte d’Alba (more than 3,000 bottles of Barolo).

The commando teams operate with the precision of special forces, studying where and when to strike. They disable alarm systems. They select their target wines with pinpoint precision. And then they sell the goods on black markets.

The wave of thefts is also taking a heavy toll on high-end restaurants. Over the years, thieves have plundered some of Italy’s most important Michelin-starred restaurants and wine shops.

At Caino in Montemerano, bottles worth €80,000 were taken (March 2025) after the thieves dug their way into the vault. At L’Orso Grigio in Ronzone, 768 bottles were reported missing, worth more than €35,000, and three former employees are on trial over the case.

At La Cantina di Soncino, around €40,000 worth in wine, food and equipment was stolen. And there was the spectacular theft at L’Affinatore in Milan, where 19 bottles of Romanée-Conti worth more than €280,000 were taken in June 2026.

Made-to-order raids like these are not confined to Italy; they have spread across Europe. The 2022 break-in at the two-Michelin-starred Coque restaurant in Madrid caused a stir after a highly specialised gang managed to gain access through the adjoining pharmacy, which was closed at the time. The haul: 132 collectible bottles worth between €150,000 and €200,000.

In Paris, an inventory carried out in January 2024 at the restaurant La Tour d’Argent found 83 bottles missing, including Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, worth around €1.5 million. They had vanished with no sign of forced entry.

items.title: Pinocchio, the trickster
items.summary: Nearly 150 years after Carlo Collodi brought him to life, the wooden puppet continues to fascinate us with his story, which Italo Calvino considered the only Gothic novel in Italian literature.
items.content:
As a child, Pinocchio is “wild”: a megalomaniac enfant terrible, cruel, cheeky, vulgar, unpredictable, quarrelsome and, at times, even touching. He is undoubtedly the forerunner of a whole tribe of unruly children, from those who populate Dickens’s novels and Mark Twain’s stories, such as Huckleberry Finn, to Pippi Longstocking and Holden Caulfield. But there is another Pinocchio, his double, inhabiting that unyielding wooden body and drawing his strength from the chthonic world that lies beneath his feet.

Pinocchio, Collodi’s extraordinary creation, whose first appearance in Giornale per i bambini 145 years ago has just been celebrated (along with the 200th anniversary of his creator’s birth), is therefore a trickster: literally a deceiver, a swindler or, in mythological terms, a “divine rogue”. He belongs to that breed of demigods whose actions create worlds only to destroy them moments later, drawn to the great chaos of existence, in which they feel at home despite everything.

Pinocchio is ignorant, like every trickster in the tales: the puppet knows everything and, at the same time, knows absolutely nothing.

To be a rogue is to be deceitful, but not out of cruelty or malice. Rather, it is because such creatures simply cannot be anything else. Pinocchio is ignorant, like every trickster in the tales collected by ethnographers: the puppet knows everything and, at the same time, knows absolutely nothing.

That is why he is sent to school. Not merely because he is a wild, impetuous, uncontrollable boy who ought to learn some manners, but also to temper his own divine ignorance, a quality that everyone else fears. Indeed, in his adventures he moves freely among monstrous beings such as Mangiafuoco, the fearsome puppet master, and the repulsive Little Man of Butter, as well as talking animals — crickets, snails, dogs, cats, foxes, birds and fish — that inhabit his mysterious kingdom.

Even the Fairy herself, with the extraordinary entourage she brings along whenever the scene changes, is in fact monstrous despite her reassuring appearance, though she never truly abandons him. She is as ambivalent as her protégé — or rather, her godson.

At the Great Puppet Theatre, where Harlequin and Pulcinella, his brothers, perform, they recognise him immediately. They know his name and his exploits before he has even begun to carry them out. When Harlequin sees him enter the theatre, he exclaims: “Heavens above! Am I dreaming or am I awake? Why, that fellow over there is Pinocchio…”

Italo Calvino saw The Story of a Puppet as a “Gothic novel”, the only one in Italian literature. Its world contains coffins, disreputable inns, hangings, the silent cart bound for the Land of Toys, muffled assassins and other sinister episodes, such as the announcement of the House of the Dead.

Elémire Zolla, a distinguished scholar of esotericism, went so far as to identify the “beautiful little girl with turquoise hair” as none other than a reincarnation of Isis, one of the principal Egyptian deities, whose mystery cult had spread throughout the Mediterranean.

Everything is magical in the Tuscan-like landscape through which the puppet travels on foot, including the stormy sea and the terrible Shark, which is none other than the whale that swallowed Jonah.

As Pietro Citati wrote in these very pages, Pinocchio’s transformation into a flesh-and-blood boy at the end of the story conceals “many hidden things”.

Pinocchio’s transformation into a flesh-and-blood boy at the end of the story conceals “many hidden things”.

The puppet had longed to spend his life with both a father and a mother, but that is not what happens. The Fairy with Turquoise Hair never becomes his earthly mother. Instead, she disappears as the fairy tale itself fades away.

With her departure, the transformations cease, along with the constant changes of shape and identity. Everything around him settles into place. The labyrinth of enchantments has dissolved and no longer hangs over him.

Now that he is a real boy, he can look at his former self, propped against a chair: “His head turned to one side, his arms dangling and his legs crossed and bent in the middle, so that it seemed a miracle he could stand upright.”

He concludes: “How funny I was when I was a puppet! And how happy I am now to have become a good little boy!”

No longer will Pinocchio leap about on those little wooden legs across the boards of the Great Puppet Theatre, acting out his own story. Nor will he race headlong through the world with his enemies in pursuit. The metamorphosis of life is complete.

It is a much-debated ending, but how could it have been otherwise? The beauty of the story lies, of course, not in its conclusion but in everything that precedes it, and in the very way the book tells its tale.

As Calvino wrote, it lies in “the inner necessity of its rhythm, of its syntax of images and metamorphoses, which means that one episode must follow another in a propulsive chain”.

This is the source of Pinocchio’s “generative power”, the quality that makes it a “model of adventure storytelling”, a book that every writer in the Italian language encounters as a first reading experience and in which each recognises something of their own wildness.

Whether told or read aloud by others, or explored directly, it is often encountered even before a child has learned to spell out the letters.

Pinocchio is not merely a story we read, but a story that reads us through its unfathomable adventures, as Giorgio Manganelli, one of its great commentators, might have said.

Could all this have something to do with that famous interruption on 29 October 1881, when Collodi abandoned his creation hanging from the Great Oak, a rope around his neck, while a cruel wind tossed him back and forth without respite?

As we know, Collodi resumed the story on 16 February 1882, prompted by the urgent requests of his young readers and perhaps inspired by a host of new ideas.

And so this book, written at two different speeds, became one of the most widely read in the world, with its extraordinary child who is both one and two.

items.title: Federica Pellegrini: ‘How a quattro stagioni pizza helped me break a record’
items.summary: The Italian swimming champion recalls her childhood training sessions at dawn, her breathing difficulties and the dark days of stress — and reveals her secrets for overcoming it
items.content:
Night opens unexpected doorways through insurmountable obstacles—bringing us to places we thought were out of reach. It offers the chance to find, or rediscover, a fresh start.

Olympic champion Federica Pellegrini began training through the winter as a young girl in La Gazzera, a suburb of Venice. It was the era of her first double training sessions. Outside, it was still dark. She was twelve years old.

What do you remember about those early morning swims? "It was extremely early, before going to school. The alarm went off at five-thirty. My mother used to drive me. By six, I was in the water. It was still pitch-black outside. I would swim until eight, then get out and change. By the time I walked into the classroom, I was completely spent."

Like so many elite athletes—Simone Biles comes to mind—you quickly found yourself under immense pressure. In November 2008, you experienced breathing difficulties during an 800-metre race. What went through your mind?

"The feeling at that moment was one of drowning, of simply not being able to breathe. And being unable to breathe underwater is an experience I wouldn't wish on anyone."

So what was really going on? "I had no idea I was asthmatic. I had pulmonary vasoconstriction triggered by certain agents in the pool."

From then on, you took every precaution and started seeing a sports psychologist, yet the crises kept happening. A few months later, on 6 March 2009, you suffered another breakdown during the 400-metre heats. What do you recall? "I fled the deck just moments before stepping onto the starting block. Once again, I felt my throat closing up. Yet physically, there was no underlying reason. I was taking standard asthma inhalers. Everything was under control, but it still wasn't working."

You kept working with your psychologist and coach. Shortly after, in July, the World Aquatics Championships in Rome were approaching—a crucial milestone. The pressure was mounting. Then something happened. One night in May 2009, you fell asleep and had a dream. What was it? "I was on the starting block for this damned 400-metre race, but I suddenly realised I was still wearing my bathrobe. Just as the whistle blew for us to take our marks. There was no time to take it off."

And what did you do? "I dived in, bathrobe and all, and started swimming. In my mind, I could see my rivals pulling away, one by one. In a normal situation, that would have caused me immense stress. Instead, I felt calm. Completely in control of myself."

Meanwhile, the bathrobe was getting heavier and heavier… "It was soaking up more and more water. But I kept going, one stroke at a time. In the dream, I managed to finish that 400 metres, and the moment I touched the wall, shortly after, I woke up."

What did you feel at dawn that morning? "Deep down, I knew I had finally come through the darkness. Not that I was completely cured, but that from then on, I would be able to manage the problem. It was an incredibly powerful dream."

At the Rome World Championships, athletes were staying at the Acqua Acetosa sports centre. On the morning of Sunday 26 July, you swam the 400-metre heats at the Foro Italico. Afterwards, you felt feverish, but didn’t take your temperature. What did you do?

"I rested, even though everything in Rome was harder. It was difficult to even eat because of the tension, and everyone was expecting me to win the two gold medals I had missed out on at Beijing 2008. The pool felt like a football stadium—something completely unprecedented for a swimmer. Everything felt massive and terrifying."

The final was in the late afternoon. There were so many people that even the pool water seemed to vibrate. You set a new world record, becoming the first woman to break the four-minute barrier. What were your thoughts after everything you had endured?

"A huge sigh of relief. I realised I could make it. But not everything was behind me. An episode like that changes you deep down. I never swam the 400 metres with complete freedom again. But it was a wonderful redemption, because back then, mental health wasn't part of the conversation. I was seen as the crazy one at the time."

It didn't end there. On Wednesday 29 July came the 200-metre event. In the afternoon, temperatures hovered near 35 degrees. By evening it cooled down, but lying in bed that night, you couldn't sleep.

"I remember that evening as if it were yesterday. The tension had dropped, yet I was tossing and turning in bed, overcome by the kind of hunger that keeps you awake. So I got up, trying to be as quiet as possible so as not to wake my roommates, and called my mother. My parents were in Rome having dinner with friends at a pizzeria. Within fifteen minutes, they arrived with two pizzas. They were cold, but they were delicious."

"I had a quattro stagioni . I was starving... I ate the pizza straight out of the box, sitting on the steps of the corridor outside our rooms at the Acqua Acetosa sports centre, with my parents beside me. By midnight, I was back in bed, sleeping peacefully on a full stomach."

Late the following afternoon, you broke the world record in the 200-metre freestyle—a record that held for 14 years. Can you tell us how you celebrated that night?

"I didn't celebrate, because I still had a relay race ahead of me. And as long as you're competing, you don't celebrate. Afterwards, on the final night, we certainly made up for lost time."

"Not often, but whenever I do, I relive every bit of it, exactly as I felt it back then."
